title: Sharps and body fluids: policy, reporting and records
audience: Workers who may come across sharps or body fluids while cleaning, and the supervisors who decide who may clean them up, in any cleaning-group business. This lesson covers the policy rules, the reporting duties and the records. The clean-up method itself is in “Body fluid spill and sharps clean-up (high-risk: trained workers only)”, and only trained workers may carry it out.
learningOutcomes: State the policy rules for sharps and body fluids that apply before any clean-up starts.
Describe the stop-and-report steps to take when a sharp or an unexpected fluid is found.
Describe the reporting and record steps after an injury, a near miss or a spill, including what the supervisor must record.
Explain why only trained workers may carry out the “Body fluid spill and sharps clean-up (high-risk: trained workers only)” clean-up, and what an untrained worker does instead.

instruction.heading: Status of this lesson
instruction.body: The uploaded source gives the heading of the sharps and body fluids annex but not its text. This lesson is a team-written overview that sits alongside the clean-up procedure in “Body fluid spill and sharps clean-up (high-risk: trained workers only)”. When the annex text is supplied, this lesson must be checked against it and corrected wherever the two differ. Nothing in this lesson grants a licence, a certificate or any authority to handle clinical waste or to carry out post-exposure care.

instruction.heading: Stop before you touch
instruction.body: The most common risk with a sharp is that it cannot be seen. Do not reach into rubbish, bedding, gaps behind furniture, or the gaps in a bin to find it. Stop, keep your hands away from the item, and call your supervisor. If you have a cut or broken skin on your hand, seal it under a waterproof dressing, and only then put on gloves. Do not handle the item until you are cleared to do so.

instruction.heading: Who may clean up
instruction.body: Only workers who have been trained for body fluid and sharps clean-up may carry out the procedure in “Body fluid spill and sharps clean-up (high-risk: trained workers only)”. Any other worker stops, keeps people away from the area, and reports the event. Making an area safe is different from clearing it. The supervisor decides who clears the area, and records the decision.

instruction.heading: Containers and waste
instruction.body: Sharps go into a rigid, labelled sharps container, and never into general waste or a loose sack. The container is set down where it cannot tip, and it is kept locked away between jobs. Body fluid waste and contaminated materials go into the clinical waste route the business uses.

instruction.heading: Injuries and near misses
instruction.body: If a sharp cuts or punctures your skin, wash the wound straight away, tell your supervisor, and get the first-aid and medical care that the business's process sets out. Record the time, the item, the place and the names of any witnesses. A near miss is reported in the same way, even when no injury happens. Reporting does not mean you caused the problem. It lets the business remove the hazard.

instruction.heading: What the supervisor records
instruction.body: For each sharps or bodily fluid event, the supervisor records what happened, the clean-up that was done, who did it and what training they held, the disposal route, and any follow-up care that was arranged.

instruction.heading: Legal and regulatory position
instruction.body: The duties for storing, transporting and disposing of sharps and clinical waste, and the response required after an exposure, vary by state and territory and by the type of premises. None of these is confirmed in this lesson. The rules that apply must be checked before this policy is used on any site.

procedure: Stop as soon as you find a sharp or an unexpected fluid, and keep your hands away from it.
Keep other people away from the area, mark it, and call your supervisor.
Check whether you have been trained for body fluid and sharps clean-up. If you have not, do not clean it up.
If you have an open cut or broken skin, seal it under a waterproof dressing, and only then put on gloves.
Only a trained worker uses the “Body fluid spill and sharps clean-up (high-risk: trained workers only)” procedure, with the equipment and protective equipment that procedure lists.
Place each sharp in a rigid sharps container. Never place a sharp in general waste.
Put contaminated materials and used protective equipment into the clinical waste route. Do not put them in general waste.
If you are injured or have a near miss, wash the wound, report to your supervisor, and get the care the process sets out.
The supervisor completes the event record and confirms the disposal route.
Seal the sharps container, lock it in its storage place, and check that it is closed before the shift finishes.

workedExamples.situation: While emptying a bin in an office, you feel something sharp hidden under a tissue.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop and take your hand out of the bin. Do not reach in to see what it is. Keep other people away and call your supervisor. A trained worker handles the item under “Body fluid spill and sharps clean-up (high-risk: trained workers only)”, after the supervisor has confirmed the disposal route.

workedExamples.situation: A worker who has not been trained for clean-up sees a blood spill on a washroom floor, and a colleague is about to mop it up.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop the colleague from starting, keep people out of the area, and report to the supervisor. Mopping up a spill is clean-up work, and under “Body fluid spill and sharps clean-up (high-risk: trained workers only)” only a trained worker may carry it out. The untrained worker's role is to make the area safe and to report.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner gets a scratch from a needle hidden in a gap beside a bench.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the order of actions?
workedExamples.reasoning: Wash the wound at once and tell the supervisor. Follow the first-aid and medical care steps in the business's process, and record the item, the time, the place and the witnesses. Do not carry on handling the item. The supervisor arranges the disposal route and records the event.

equipmentAndPpe: Gloves suited to the task, with eye protection where there is a risk of splashing.
Waterproof dressings for any cut or broken skin.
A rigid, labelled sharps container, kept locked away when it is stored.
Clinical waste bags, or the clinical waste route the business uses.
Grabbing tools such as grips, for trained workers only.
The business's injury and near-miss report form.

commonErrors.error: Reaching into a bin or under furniture to find a sharp.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, keep your hands out, and call your supervisor before you look.

commonErrors.error: Putting a sharp in a general waste sack because the sharps container is across the room.
commonErrors.prevention: Carry a sharps container on the job, or ask for one before you start. Never use general waste for a sharp.

commonErrors.error: Not reporting a scratch because it looks minor.
commonErrors.prevention: Report every sharps contact and every near miss, however small it looks.

commonErrors.error: An untrained worker mopping up a body fluid spill to clear the floor quickly.
commonErrors.prevention: Make the area safe, keep people away, and call a trained worker.

commonErrors.error: Working with an open cut under gloves.
commonErrors.prevention: Seal the cut under a waterproof dressing, and only then pull on the gloves.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not handle sharps or body fluid waste with bare hands, and do not reach into an area you cannot see into. Stop and report instead.

Only workers trained for body fluid and sharps clean-up may carry out the “Body fluid spill and sharps clean-up (high-risk: trained workers only)” procedure. Completing this lesson does not make a worker trained for that procedure.
Sharps and clinical waste must be contained and disposed of through the approved route.
The response after an exposure, including any testing, follow-up and notification duties, must be set by the business under the rules of the relevant jurisdiction.
This lesson does not grant one.

qualityStandard: No sharp is handled with bare hands, and no item is retrieved by hand from a gap that cannot be seen into.
Every sharp is placed in a rigid sharps container, and none is placed in general waste.
Every sharps contact, near miss and body fluid event is reported on the day it happens.
Only trained workers carry out the “Body fluid spill and sharps clean-up (high-risk: trained workers only)” clean-up, and the supervisor can show which workers are trained.
documentationEvidence: Incident or near-miss report showing the time, the place, the item, the witnesses and the first-aid steps taken.
Disposal record showing the route used and the date the sharps container was removed.
Training record for each worker who carried out a clean-up.
Supervisor follow-up record for each event, including any care that was arranged.
summary: Stop, keep your hands away, and call your supervisor when you find a sharp or an unexpected fluid.
Only a trained worker carries out the “Body fluid spill and sharps clean-up (high-risk: trained workers only)” clean-up. Everyone else makes the area safe and reports.
Sharps go into a rigid, labelled container, never into general waste.
Report every sharps contact, however small, and get care straight away.

knowledgeChecks.question: You feel something sharp in a bin, hidden under a tissue. What is the first action?
options: Reach in carefully so you can see what it is and report it
Stop, take your hand out, keep people away, and call your supervisor
Tip the bin into a sack and take it to the outside waste area

knowledgeChecks.question: Where does a used sharp go?
options: Into a general waste sack, sealed tightly
Into a cardboard box with the lid taped shut
Into the washroom bin with the paper towels
Into a rigid, labelled sharps container

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker who has not been trained for body fluid clean-up finds a blood spill on a floor. What does the worker do?
options: Make the area safe, keep people away, and report to the supervisor
Mop it up quickly so the floor is clear before customers arrive
Cover the spill with paper towels and mop it up at the end of the day
